entry: American astrophysicist, author and science communicator. Tyson has directed the Hayden Planetarium at the [[American Museum of Natural History]] in New York City since 1996, and founded the museum's Department of Astrophysics in 1997. Tyson hosted the television series *NOVA ScienceNow* on [[PBS]] from 2006 to 2011, and has hosted the weekly podcast *StarTalk* since 2009. In 2014 he hosted *Cosmos: A Spacetime Odyssey*, a successor to [[Carl Sagan]]'s 1980 series *Cosmos: A Personal Voyage*. The U.S. National Academy of Sciences gave him its Public Welfare Medal in 2015.

American investigative journalist, born Elizabeth Jane Cochran and known by the pen name Nellie Bly. Her 1885 articles for the *Pittsburgh Dispatch* argued for better jobs for women and for reform of [[Divorce|divorce]] laws. She went undercover as a poor woman to be hired at a copper cable factory, to see the working conditions of women and children firsthand. Abroad, she served as a foreign correspondent in Mexico for nearly half a year; her dispatches later appeared as *Six Months in Mexico*. She is best known for a record-breaking trip around the world in 72 days, made in emulation of [[Jules Verne]]'s fictional character Phileas Fogg, and for an undercover exposé of a mental institution. She ushered in the era of stunt girl reporting and helped advance immersion journalism.

41st vice president of the United States, under [[Gerald Ford]] (1974–77). A member of the Republican Party and the wealthy Rockefeller family, he was governor of New York from 1959 to 1973 and led the party's moderate faction. After unsuccessful bids for the Republican presidential nomination in 1960, 1964 and 1968, he was appointed vice president in December 1974. As governor he oversaw expansion of the State University of New York and construction of the Empire State Plaza in Albany. He also served as trustee and president of the [[Museum of Modern Art]].

Genus of aquatic plants with large, showy flowers, commonly called lotus. Members resemble water lilies (family Nymphaeaceae) but are only distantly related to them. The genus is ancient, with dozens of species known from fossils since the Early Cretaceous, but only two living species survive. *Nelumbo nucifera* is native to East Asia, South Asia and Southeast Asia, and *Nelumbo lutea* to North America and the Caribbean. Their leaves are highly water-repellent, a property known as the lotus effect. The flowers of Nelumbo generate heat through an alternative oxidase pathway; the most common explanation is that the heat attracts pollinators. Horticultural hybrids have been produced between the two species.

Aquatic plant, one of two living species in [[Nelumbo]], known as the sacred lotus or Indian lotus. It is the national flower of India and, unofficially, of Vietnam. It has been cultivated for c. 3,000 years for its edible seeds. Its seeds can remain viable for many years, and the oldest recorded germination came from seeds 1,300 years old recovered from a dry lakebed in northeastern China. Therefore, the Chinese regard the plant as a symbol of longevity. It is used in religious offerings, especially in Hinduism and Buddhism, and is widely depicted in art and literature.

Worm of the phylum Nematoda, also called roundworm or eelworm, with a flexible cuticle. Unlike flatworms, nematodes have a tubular digestive system with openings at both ends. They are classified with arthropods and tardigrades in the clade Ecdysozoa. Most species are free-living, feeding on microorganisms, but many are parasitic, including pathogens of most plants and animals. They are found in marine, freshwater and terrestrial environments, from the polar regions to the tropics. They make up about 80% of all individual animals on Earth. Estimates of total species range widely, but are now placed closer to one million. About 35 species are human parasites.

Fourth and penultimate stage of ancient Assyrian history (911–609 BC). At its height, the empire ruled Mesopotamia, the Levant and Egypt, as well as parts of Anatolia, Arabia, Iran and Armenia. It was the largest empire up to that time. Tiglath-Pileser III (r. 745–727 BC) reasserted royal power and more than doubled the size of the empire, conquering Babylonia and large parts of the Levant. Under Esarhaddon (r. 681–669 BC) the empire reached its largest extent through the conquest of Egypt. A policy of resettling conquered populations weakened local identities and facilitated the rise of Aramaic as the regional lingua franca. Its army made large-scale use of cavalry and new siege techniques, and its communication system used relay stations and well-maintained roads. The empire fell swiftly in the late 7th century BC, destroyed by a Babylonian uprising and an invasion by the Medes.

Post–World War II movements and ideologies that profess or idealize [[Nazism]] in whole or in part. Neo-Nazis promote the racial or ethnic supremacy of their own group, often [[White supremacy|White supremacy]], and incite hatred of minorities, frequently through [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]] and Islamophobia. Some groups seek to establish a fascist state, such as a "Fourth Reich." Holocaust denial is a common feature, as are Nazi symbols and admiration of [[Adolf Hitler]]. Neo-Nazism is considered a form of [[Far-right politics|far-right politics]]. In Germany and a number of other countries, it is prohibited by laws targeting Nazi ideology.

Revivalist style of architecture, also called Classical Revival architecture. It was produced by the Neoclassical movement, which began in the mid-18th century in Italy, France and Germany. It became one of the most prominent architectural styles in the [[Western world]]. The movement aimed to strip away the excesses of Late [[Baroque]] and return to a purer, more authentic classical style adapted to modern purposes. Archaeology and accurate published records of surviving classical buildings were crucial to its emergence. In many countries an initial wave drew essentially on Roman architecture, and from about the start of the 19th century a second wave of Greek Revival architecture followed. The style emphasizes the wall and is defined by symmetry and simple geometry rather than ornament. A version of the style continues in the 21st century as New Classical architecture.

Western cultural movement in the decorative and visual arts, literature, theater, music and architecture, inspired by classical antiquity. It emerged from the 18th-century [[Age of Enlightenment]] and reached its peak in the early to mid-19th century, when it competed with [[Romanticism]]. European Neoclassicism in the visual arts began c. 1760 in opposition to the [[Rococo]] style, which emphasized grace, ornamentation and asymmetry. Neoclassicism was born in [[Rome]], largely through the writings of Johann Joachim Winckelmann during the rediscovery of [[Pompeii]] and Herculaneum. The sculpture it embraced was more often Roman copies of Hellenistic works. The [[Empire style]], a second phase in architecture and the decorative arts, centered on Paris during the [[Napoleon|Napoleonic]] era. The movement remained influential into the 20th and 21st centuries, especially in the United States and Russia.

Silvery-white metallic element of the [[Lanthanide|lanthanide]] series, symbol Nd and atomic number 60. One of the [[Rare-earth element|rare-earth elements]], it tarnishes in air and reacts with water. Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach discovered it in 1885 by separating didymium into neodymium and praseodymium. Its name comes from the Greek for "new twin." China is the largest producer and refiner of the rare-earth elements used in [[Magnet|magnets]]. Neodymium–iron–boron magnets, which produce strong magnetic fields from small, lightweight components, are used in audio equipment, hard disk drives, electric vehicle motors and some wind turbines. Neodymium also colors glass, and its ions are the active component of solid-state lasers such as Nd:YAG lasers. Neodymium isotope ratios are used to date rocks and trace geological processes.

Second geologic period of the [[Cenozoic]], spanning 20.46 million years, from 23.04 to 2.58 million years ago. It is divided into two epochs, the earlier [[Miocene]] and the later [[Pliocene]]. The term was coined in 1853 by the Austrian paleontologist Moritz Hörnes. During this period mammals and birds evolved into modern forms, while other groups remained relatively unchanged. The first humans, *Homo habilis*, appeared in [[Africa]] near the end of the period. The most significant continental movement was the connection of North and South America at the Isthmus of Panama, late in the Pliocene. This cut off warm Pacific currents from the Atlantic, leaving only the [[Gulf Stream]] to transfer heat to the Arctic Ocean. The global climate cooled considerably throughout the period, culminating in continental glaciations in the [[Quaternary]] Period that followed.

Political and economic ideology advocating free-market capitalism. It developed from challenges to classical liberalism in the early 20th century. Its policies include lower taxes, privatization, deregulation, free trade and austerity. Scholars associated its ideas with the Mont Pelerin Society, including [[Friedrich Hayek]] and [[Milton Friedman]], and with politicians such as [[Margaret Thatcher]] and [[Ronald Reagan]]. The term entered academic use in the 1980s in association with economic reforms in [[Chile]] under [[Augusto Pinochet]], and was mainly employed by critics of market reform. Critics argue that it has contributed to class inequality and to privatization in education and health care.

Archaeological period, the last division of the Stone Age, also called the New Stone Age. It lasted from c. 10,000 BC to c. 2,000 BC in Asia, Europe and Africa. The period saw the Neolithic Revolution, a set of developments including the introduction of farming, the domestication of animals and a shift from hunter-gatherer life to settlement. Farming appeared in West Asia about 12,000 years ago, and its founder crops included wheat, lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch and flax. Independent domestication in Africa, South Asia and Southeast Asia produced regional Neolithic cultures. In West Asia the period ended with the [[Chalcolithic]], or Copper Age, marked by the development of metallurgy. [[Göbekli Tepe]], a temple area in southeastern Turkey dated to around 9500 BC, may be regarded as the beginning of the period.

Chemical element of the noble gas group, with the symbol Ne and atomic number 10. Neon is a colorless, odorless, inert gas under standard conditions, with about two-thirds the density of air. British chemists Sir William Ramsay and Morris Travers discovered it in London in 1898, identifying it by its bright red emission spectrum. The name comes from the Greek word for "new." Neon is comparatively scarce on Earth but ranks fifth in cosmic abundance, after hydrogen, helium, oxygen and carbon. Its red-orange glow is used in neon signs and in the red light of helium–neon lasers. It is obtained mainly by fractional distillation of liquid air, making it more expensive than helium.

Japanese [[Anime|anime]] television series produced by Gainax and Tatsunoko Production and directed by Hideaki Anno. It aired on TV Tokyo from October 1995 to March 1996. Set in 2015, it follows teenager Shinji Ikari, recruited to pilot a giant biomechanical mecha against beings called Angels. The series deconstructs the mecha genre and draws on [[Shinto]] cosmology, [[Kabbalah]] and the psychoanalytic ideas of [[Sigmund Freud]] and [[Carl Jung]]. Its abstract final two episodes drew controversy, and the 1997 film *The End of Evangelion* remade them. It is regarded as one of the greatest animated series of all time.

Abnormal, excessive growth of cells, often forming a mass called a tumor. Neoplasia is the process that produces a neoplasm. Its growth is uncoordinated with that of the surrounding tissue and persists even if the original trigger is removed. Benign neoplasms, such as uterine fibroids and skin moles, are localized and do not transform into cancer. Malignant neoplasms, commonly called cancers, invade and destroy surrounding tissue, may form metastases, and are the focus of [[Oncology|oncology]]. The word derives from Ancient Greek *neo* (new) and *plasma* (formation). Some neoplasms, such as [[Leukemia|leukemia]], do not form a tumor. Tumor is not synonymous with cancer, since a tumor can be benign, precancerous or malignant.

Landlocked country in South Asia, mostly in the Himalayas. Kathmandu is the capital and largest city, and the country includes eight of the world's ten highest mountains. It borders the [[Tibet Autonomous Region]] of China to the north and India to the south, east and west. It is a multi-ethnic, multilingual, multireligious and multicultural sovereign state, with Nepali as its official language. The Gorkha Kingdom unified Nepal under the Shah dynasty in the 18th century. Nepal was never colonized but served as a buffer state between imperial China and British India. Parliamentary democracy was introduced in 1951, but monarchs suspended it in 1960 and 2005. After a civil war in the 1990s and early 2000s, Nepal became a secular republic in 2008, ending the world's last Hindu monarchy. A constitution adopted in 2015 affirms the country as a federal parliamentary republic of seven provinces.

Indo-Aryan language native to the Himalayan region of South Asia, written in [[Devanagari]] script. It is the official and most widely spoken language of [[Nepal]], where it is also a [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]]. It has official status in India, including in the states of [[Sikkim]] and [[West Bengal]], and it is spoken by about a quarter of [[Bhutan]]. Overall it has approximately 19 million native speakers and an additional 14 million second-language speakers. The language originated in the Sinja Valley, the capital of the Khasa Kingdom around the 10th and 14th centuries. Its earliest known inscription, at Dullu in Dailekh District, dates to around 981 CE. In the 19th century Bhanubhakta Acharya translated the [[Ramayana]] into Nepali, a version popular for its colloquial flavor and religious sincerity.

Enigmatic figures in the [[Hebrew Bible]] and later Jewish and Christian literature, traditionally linked with great size. The earliest reference, in Genesis 6:1–4, connects them to "mighty men of old" and to unions between the "sons of God" and the "daughters of men." The term may derive from a Hebrew root meaning "to fall," and the Septuagint translated it as *gigantes*, or [[Giant|giants]]. Numbers 13:33 describes descendants of the Nephilim in Canaan, though some scholars see the spies' report as exaggerated. In Second Temple literature such as *1 Enoch*, they are offspring of rebellious [[Angel|angels]] and human women.

Radioactive [[Actinide|actinide]] metal with the symbol Np and atomic number 93. It is the first transuranic element and is named after the planet [[Neptune]], beyond [[Uranus]]. It was first synthesized by Edwin McMillan and Philip H. Abelson at the Berkeley Radiation Laboratory in 1940, although many false claims of its discovery had been made earlier. Most neptunium is now made as a by-product of neutron irradiation of uranium in nuclear reactors. It has no commercial uses at present, but it is a precursor of plutonium-238, which is used in radioisotope thermal generators for spacecraft. Like all actinides, it is radioactive, poisonous and pyrophoric, and it can accumulate in bones.

Roman emperor (r. AD 54–68) and final emperor of the [[Julio-Claudian dynasty]]. [[Claudius]] adopted him as heir after marrying his mother, Agrippina the Younger. Nero succeeded Claudius in AD 54. Early in his reign he was guided by his mother, his tutor [[Seneca the Younger]] and the praetorian prefect Burrus. Roman sources also implicate him in the deaths of his mother, his wife Claudia Octavia and his stepbrother Britannicus. He ordered the construction of amphitheaters and promoted athletic games, and he made public appearances as an actor, poet, musician and charioteer. His reign included a Roman–Parthian War (58–63), the suppression of a revolt in Britain led by [[Boudica]], and the start of the First Jewish–Roman War. After the senator Vindex rebelled with support from Galba, Nero was declared a public enemy, fled Rome and committed suicide. [[Tacitus]] claims Nero blamed [[Christians]] for the Great Fire of Rome.

Dynasty of seven [[Roman emperor|Roman emperors]] who ruled from AD 96 to 192. Its first five emperors, Nerva, [[Trajan]], [[Hadrian]], Antoninus Pius and [[Marcus Aurelius]], are known as the "Five Good Emperors." In the first five of six successions the reigning emperor had no male heir and adopted a successor. Under Roman law, adoption created a bond as strong as kinship. The label derives from [[Niccolò Machiavelli]]'s *The Discourses on Livy*, which judged the adopted emperors good. Marcus Aurelius named his son Commodus as heir, a choice regarded as the beginning of the empire's decline. The dynasty ended with Commodus's murder in 192, followed by the Year of the Five Emperors.

Main tissue component of the [[Nervous system|nervous system]], also called neural tissue. It is composed of [[Neuron|neurons]], which receive and transmit impulses, and neuroglia, which support them and help propagate impulses. Each neuron has an axon, a long projection that sends action potentials to the next cell. Bundles of axons form nerves in the [[Peripheral nervous system|peripheral nervous system]] and tracts in the [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]]. Functions of the nervous system are sensory input, integration, control of muscles and glands, homeostasis and mental activity. Neurons are classified by function as sensory, motor or interneurons, and by structure as multipolar, bipolar or pseudounipolar. Astrocytes are the most abundant cell type in the brain, and oligodendrocytes form myelin in the central nervous system.

Swiss multinational food and drink company, headquartered in Vevey. It was formed in 1905 by the merger of the Anglo-Swiss Condensed Milk Company, founded in 1866, and the company founded in 1867 by Henri Nestlé, which sold milk-based baby food. Its products include [[Coffee|coffee]], confectionery, bottled water, infant formula, dairy, frozen foods and pet food. It has been the largest publicly held food company in the world by revenue since 2014, and its brands include Nescafé, Kit Kat and Maggi. Its promotion of infant formula in developing countries led to a boycott in the 1970s, with critics blaming it for discouraging [[Breastfeeding|breastfeeding]] and for the deaths of over 10 million infants. It has also faced criticism over labor and [[Deforestation|deforestation]] linked to West African cocoa, water extraction and plastic pollution.
